title: Right Triangle Trigonometry with SOHCAHTOA
description: Sketch and label SAT right triangles, choose and solve exact sine, cosine, and tangent equations, manage degree and radian mode, and transfer trig ratios across similar triangles.

blocks.html:
Turn point and side labels into one trig equation

The move: Sketch it and label from the angle you're using.

Why it pays: The SAT names vertices, not "opposite" and "adjacent," so the sketch does the translating — and then choosing sine, cosine, or tangent is mechanical.

One caution: "Adjacent" never means the hypotenuse, even though the hypotenuse also touches the angle — and check that the calculator is in degrees.

SAT questions usually name vertices and sides, not “opposite” or “adjacent.” Your first job is to sketch the right triangle, place the point labels, and identify each side relative to the given acute angle.

You will use that labeled sketch to choose sine, cosine, or tangent, isolate the requested side in exact form, and manage Desmos angle mode. At the end, you will connect the same ratios to similar triangles.

Goal: Translate SAT point labels into a reliable diagram and an exact SOHCAHTOA expression.

Start with the marked angle and point labels

Inspect \(\triangle ABC\). It is right at \(C\), and the acute angle being used is \(\angle B=\theta\). The side names come from those two facts.

First look: Find the right-angle vertex and the acute-angle vertex before naming any side.

content.prompt: Which description always identifies the hypotenuse of a right triangle?
choices: The side directly below the marked acute angle
The shortest side in the drawing
The side opposite whichever angle is labeled \(\theta\)
content.hint: The hypotenuse is defined using the right angle, not the location or rotation of the drawing.
content.explanation: Correct. The hypotenuse is always across from the \(90^\circ\) angle, and it is the triangle's longest side.

blocks.html:
Opposite and adjacent depend on the acute angle

The hypotenuse never changes: it is across from the right angle.

The other two labels depend on the acute angle you are using:

  • Opposite: the side across from the marked acute angle.
  • Adjacent: the non-hypotenuse side touching the marked acute angle.

If the question switches to the other acute angle, opposite and adjacent switch places. The hypotenuse stays the same.

Watch out: “Adjacent” never means the hypotenuse, even though the hypotenuse also touches the angle.

content.prompt: A right triangle's two legs are \(AB\) and \(BC\), and its hypotenuse is \(AC\). Relative to acute angle \(A\), which side is opposite?
content.hint: The opposite side does not touch angle A.
content.explanation: Right. Side \(BC\) sits across from angle \(A\). Side \(AB\) is adjacent, and \(AC\) is the hypotenuse.

blocks.html:
Build your own reference sketch from the words

A problem may say: “In right triangle \(PQR\), angle \(Q\) is a right angle and \(\angle R=32^\circ\).” Turn that sentence into a quick sketch:

  1. Draw any right triangle. It does not need to be to scale.
  2. Put \(Q\) at the right-angle vertex.
  3. Put \(R\) at one acute vertex and label it \(32^\circ\).
  4. Put \(P\) at the remaining vertex.
  5. Label the sides from \(\angle R\): \(PQ\) is opposite, \(QR\) is adjacent, and \(PR\) is the hypotenuse.

SAT habit: Copy every point, angle, and side label onto your sketch before choosing a trig function.

content.prompt: In right triangle \(PQR\), \(\angle Q=90^\circ\), and the trig angle is \(\angle R\). After making a sketch, how should you label the sides relative to \(\angle R\)?
content.hint: The side across from the right angle at Q is the hypotenuse. Then look across from angle R.
content.explanation: Correct. \(PR\) is across from the right angle, \(PQ\) is across from angle \(R\), and \(QR\) is the remaining leg touching angle \(R\).

blocks.html:
SOHCAHTOA stores the three ratios

For an acute angle \(\theta\) in a right triangle:

  • SOH: \(\sin(\theta)=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\)
  • CAH: \(\cos(\theta)=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\)
  • TOA: \(\tan(\theta)=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\)

Mnemonic: SOH = sine, opposite, hypotenuse; CAH = cosine, adjacent, hypotenuse; TOA = tangent, opposite, adjacent.

content.prompt: In right triangle \(PQR\), \(\angle Q=90^\circ\), and the angle being used is \(\angle R\). The question gives \(QR\) and asks for \(PQ\). Which trig function should you use?
content.hint: On your sketch, \(PQ\) is opposite angle R and \(QR\) is adjacent.
content.explanation: Correct. The point labels translate to opposite and adjacent, so TOA gives \(\tan(R)=PQ/QR\).

blocks.html:
A five-step process

  1. Sketch. Draw a right triangle and copy the vertex labels.
  2. Mark. Place the right angle, the given acute angle, known lengths, and the requested side.
  3. Relabel. Write opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse beside the point-labeled sides.
  4. Choose and solve. Pick SOH, CAH, or TOA from the known and requested sides, then isolate the requested side.
  5. Keep it exact. Select the matching trig expression unless the question explicitly requests an approximation.

Decision rule: Your reference sketch translates SAT labels into the two side names that choose the trig function.

Set Desmos to the angle mode the question uses

Desmos opens in Radians mode by default. Most SAT right-triangle diagrams label angles in degrees, such as \(35^\circ\).

Open Graph Settings, find Angle Measure, and manually select Degrees before evaluating trig with a degree angle. Switch back to Radians when the problem gives a radian measure.

Test-day habit: Check the angle mode before the first trig calculation and whenever the question changes units.

content.prompt: A triangle labels an acute angle as \(35^\circ\). What should you do before typing \(\tan(35)\) in Desmos?
choices: Open Graph Settings and select Degrees
Leave Desmos in its default Radians mode
content.hint: The degree symbol tells you how Desmos must interpret 35.
content.explanation: Exactly. Select Degrees so Desmos treats 35 as \(35^\circ\), not 35 radians.

blocks.html:
Model 1: translate the labels, then use tangent

In right triangle \(ABC\), \(\angle C=90^\circ\), \(\angle A=35^\circ\), \(AC=12\), and \(BC=x\).

Make a sketch. From \(\angle A\), \(BC\) is opposite and \(AC\) is adjacent. Therefore:

\[\tan(35^\circ)=\frac{BC}{AC}=\frac{x}{12}.\]

Multiply by \(12\):

\[x=12\tan(35^\circ).\]

This trig expression is the exact side length. A decimal is only an approximation.

Exact answer: \(BC=12\tan(35^\circ)\).

content.prompt: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle C=90^\circ\), \(\angle A=35^\circ\), \(AC=12\), and \(BC=x\). Which equation is correct?
content.hint: Sketch the triangle. From angle A, BC is opposite and AC is adjacent.
content.explanation: Correct. The point labels become opposite \(BC=x\) over adjacent \(AC=12\).

content.prompt: Which is the exact value of \(BC\) in the previous triangle?
content.solution:
Start from the equation for this triangle: from \(\angle A\), \(BC=x\) is opposite and \(AC=12\) is adjacent, so \(\tan(35^\circ)=\frac{x}{12}\).
Multiply both sides by \(12\) to isolate the requested side: \(x=12\tan(35^\circ)\).
Keep it exact: the trig expression is the exact length, and a decimal is only an approximation.
So the answer is choice B, \(12\tan(35^\circ)\).
content.hint: Solve \(\tan(35^\circ)=x/12\) for x without converting the trig value to a decimal.
content.explanation: Right. Multiplying both sides by \(12\) gives the exact result \(BC=12\tan(35^\circ)\).

blocks.html:
Model 2: identify the hypotenuse from the right angle

In right triangle \(XYZ\), \(\angle Y=90^\circ\), \(\angle X=28^\circ\), \(YZ=9\), and \(XZ=h\).

On your sketch, \(XZ\) lies across from the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse. Relative to \(\angle X\), \(YZ\) is opposite. Use SOH:

\[\sin(28^\circ)=\frac{YZ}{XZ}=\frac9h.\]

Isolate the hypotenuse:

\[h=\frac9{\sin(28^\circ)}.\]

Exact answer: \(XZ=\dfrac9{\sin(28^\circ)}\).

content.prompt: In \(\triangle XYZ\), \(\angle Y=90^\circ\), \(\angle X=28^\circ\), \(YZ=9\), and \(XZ=h\). Which equation is correct?
content.hint: The side across from the right angle at Y is XZ. From angle X, YZ is opposite.
content.explanation: Correct. The point-labeled sides translate to opposite \(YZ=9\) over hypotenuse \(XZ=h\).

content.prompt: Which is the exact value of \(XZ\)?
content.solution:
Start from the equation for this triangle: \(XZ=h\) is the hypotenuse and \(YZ=9\) is opposite \(\angle X\), so \(\sin(28^\circ)=\frac{9}{h}\).
The unknown begins in the denominator, so multiply both sides by \(h\): \(h\sin(28^\circ)=9\).
Divide both sides by \(\sin(28^\circ)\): \(h=\frac{9}{\sin(28^\circ)}\).
Keep it exact rather than converting to a decimal.
So the answer is choice A, \(\frac{9}{\sin(28^\circ)}\).
content.hint: Label the sides from the \(28^\circ\) angle: which role does the given \(9\) play, and which does the unknown play? Set up that ratio and watch where the unknown starts.
content.explanation: Correct. Multiplying by h and dividing by \(\sin(28^\circ)\) gives \(XZ=9/\sin(28^\circ)\).

blocks.html:
Guided variation: translate a new set of point labels

In right triangle \(PQR\), \(\angle Q=90^\circ\), \(\angle P=41^\circ\), \(PR=18\), and \(PQ=a\).

Sketch it before continuing. The right angle makes \(PR\) the hypotenuse. Relative to \(\angle P\), \(PQ\) is adjacent. Use CAH:

\[\cos(41^\circ)=\frac{PQ}{PR}=\frac{a}{18}.\]

Therefore:

\[a=18\cos(41^\circ).\]

Keep it exact: The requested side is \(18\cos(41^\circ)\), not a rounded decimal.

content.prompt: For the point-labeled triangle above, which is the exact value of \(PQ\)?
content.hint: From angle P, PQ is adjacent and PR is the hypotenuse. Solve \(\cos(41^\circ)=a/18\).
content.explanation: Correct. CAH gives \(\cos(41^\circ)=PQ/18\), so \(PQ=18\cos(41^\circ)\).

blocks.html:
Four checks catch most trig errors

  • Sketch check: Did you put the right angle and acute angle at the correct named vertices?
  • Side check: Did you relabel opposite and adjacent from the angle actually being used?
  • Order check: Does the ratio follow SOHCAHTOA in the correct numerator-denominator order?
  • Exact-form check: Did you stop at the exact trig expression instead of replacing it with a rounded decimal?

If you use Desmos to inspect a value, also match its Degrees or Radians setting to the problem.

Do not trust the picture's orientation: The named vertices—not left, right, top, or bottom—determine every side role.

content.prompt: Which sequence is safest for a right-triangle trig question?
choices: Choose the trig function from the angle's printed size, label the three sides afterward to confirm, and round to a decimal early.
Start with sine each time, enter the given numbers directly, and replace the exact form with the first decimal that Desmos shows.
Find the longest-looking side in the drawing, assume the current angle mode is correct, and multiply the two given values together.
Sketch and place the named vertices, mark the angles and sides, translate the sides into opposite/adjacent/hypotenuse, choose the ratio, solve, and keep the exact form.
content.hint: The reference sketch and side translation must come before the trig-function choice.
content.explanation: Exactly. That sequence makes the point labels choose the ratio and preserves the SAT's usual exact answer form.

blocks.html:
Degrees and radians measure the same turns

Degrees and radians are two units for measuring angles. One half-turn can be written either way:

\[180^\circ=\pi\text{ radians}.\]

That equality creates both conversion factors.

Anchor: \(180^\circ\leftrightarrow\pi\) radians and \(360^\circ\leftrightarrow2\pi\) radians.

Convert degrees to radians

Multiply by \(\pi/180\) so the degree unit cancels:

Degrees to radians: \(\text{degrees}\times\dfrac{\pi}{180}\)

For \(150^\circ\):

\[150\cdot\frac{\pi}{180}=\frac{5\pi}{6}.\]

Reduce the fraction, and keep \(\pi\) for an exact answer.

content.prompt: What is \(225^\circ\) in radians?
content.hint: Multiply 225 by \(\pi/180\), then reduce \(225/180\).

blocks.html:
Convert radians to degrees

Reverse the conversion factor:

Radians to degrees: \(\text{radians}\times\dfrac{180}{\pi}\)

For \(7\pi/12\):

\[\frac{7\pi}{12}\cdot\frac{180}{\pi}=7\cdot15=105^\circ.\]

The \(\pi\) cancels, leaving degrees.

content.prompt: What is \(11\pi/6\) radians in degrees?
content.hint: Multiply \(11\pi/6\) by \(180/\pi\).
content.explanation: Right. The \(\pi\) cancels, and \(11\cdot180/6=330^\circ\).

blocks.html:
Changing mode is not the same as converting

Angle mode tells Desmos how to interpret a number inside a trig function.

  • In Degrees mode, \(\sin(30)\) means \(\sin(30^\circ)=\frac12\).
  • In Radians mode, \(\sin(\pi/6)=\frac12\).

Both entries describe the same angle because \(30^\circ=\pi/6\). Typing \(\sin(30)\) in Radians mode describes a different angle.

Match the entry to the mode: Degrees mode for \(30\); Radians mode for \(\pi/6\).

content.prompt: Which setup correctly evaluates the sine of a \(30^\circ\) angle?
choices: Type \(\sin(30)\) while Desmos remains in its default Radians mode.
Use Degrees mode and type \(\sin(30)\), or use Radians mode and type \(\sin(\pi/6)\).
Use Degrees mode and type \(\sin(\pi/6)\) for the same angle.
Angle mode does not affect the values that trig functions return.
content.hint: Either keep 30 as degrees or convert it to the equivalent radian measure \(\pi/6\).
content.explanation: Correct. Both matching setups produce the exact value \(1/2\). The entry and selected angle mode must describe the same angle.

blocks.html:
Similar right triangles share trig values

Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

Because a trig function is a ratio of two sides, scaling both sides by the same factor does not change the ratio. Therefore, equal corresponding acute angles have equal sine, cosine, and tangent values.

Key idea: Similar triangles can have different side lengths but the same corresponding trig ratios.

Connect corresponding angles and ratios

In the diagram, \(\angle B\) corresponds to \(\angle F\). The triangles are different sizes and orientations, but those angles are equal.

For the blue angles:

\[\sin(B)=\frac{AC}{BC}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sin(F)=\frac{DE}{FE}.\]

The corresponding side ratios are equal, so \(\sin(B)=\sin(F)\). The same reasoning works for cosine and tangent.

content.prompt: Two right triangles are similar, and acute angle \(P\) corresponds to acute angle \(X\). Which statement must be true?
choices: Each side length in the first triangle equals a side length in the second.
\(\sin(P)\) is multiplied by the triangles' scale factor to become \(\sin(X)\).
Only the hypotenuse ratio remains equal.
content.hint: Corresponding angles are equal, and scaling both sides in a ratio leaves the ratio unchanged.
content.explanation: Exactly. Equal corresponding angles have the same three trig values even when the triangles have different side lengths.

content.prompt: Every side of a right triangle is doubled to create a similar triangle. What happens to the tangent of a corresponding acute angle?
choices: It is doubled, growing along with the two doubled side lengths.
It is cut in half, since the ratio now involves larger sides.
It stays the same because both opposite and adjacent are doubled.
It becomes \(90^\circ\), matching the enlarged right angle.
content.hint: Write \(2\cdot\text{opposite}/(2\cdot\text{adjacent})\) and simplify.
content.explanation: Correct. The scale factor cancels from the ratio, so tangent stays the same.

blocks.html:
Combined model: translate two triangles

Right triangles \(ABC\) and \(DEF\) are similar, with \(A\leftrightarrow D\), \(B\leftrightarrow E\), and \(C\leftrightarrow F\). Also, \(\angle C=\angle F=90^\circ\), \(\angle A=38^\circ\), \(AC=10\), and \(DF=25\). Find \(EF\).

Sketch both triangles and preserve the correspondence. From \(\angle A\), \(BC\) is opposite and \(AC\) is adjacent:

\[BC=10\tan(38^\circ).\]

The large-to-small scale factor is \(DF/AC=25/10\). Because \(BC\leftrightarrow EF\):

\[EF=(10\tan(38^\circ))\left(\frac{25}{10}\right).\]

Keep it exact: Do not round the small triangle before scaling.

The corresponding angle gives an exact shortcut

Since \(A\leftrightarrow D\), \(\angle D=38^\circ\). In the larger triangle, \(EF\) is opposite \(\angle D\) and \(DF=25\) is adjacent:

\[\tan(38^\circ)=\frac{EF}{25}.\]

Therefore:

\[EF=25\tan(38^\circ).\]

This equals the two-step expression because

\[(10\tan(38^\circ))\left(\frac{25}{10}\right)=25\tan(38^\circ).\]

SAT choice: Solve one triangle and scale, or transfer the corresponding angle and use trig directly. Both routes should simplify to the same exact expression.

content.prompt: Which expression correctly uses \(\triangle ABC\) and then scales its side \(BC\) to the corresponding side \(EF\)?
content.hint: Two decisions: from angle \(A\), which ratio connects the labeled side to \(BC\)? And for the \(ABC\)-to-\(DEF\) direction, which triangle's side belongs on top of the scale factor?
content.explanation: Correct. \(BC=10\tan(38^\circ)\), and the scale factor from \(ABC\) to \(DEF\) is \(25/10\).

content.prompt: Which is the simplified exact value of \(EF\)?
content.solution:
One route solves the small triangle and scales: \(BC=10\tan(38^\circ)\), and the scale factor to \(\triangle DEF\) is \(25/10\), so \(EF=(10\tan(38^\circ))(25/10)=25\tan(38^\circ)\).
The other route transfers the corresponding angle: \(A\leftrightarrow D\) gives \(\angle D=38^\circ\), and in \(\triangle DEF\), \(EF\) is opposite with \(DF=25\) adjacent, so \(\tan(38^\circ)=EF/25\) and \(EF=25\tan(38^\circ)\).
Both routes simplify to the same exact expression.
So the answer is choice B, \(25\tan(38^\circ)\).
content.hint: Simplify \((10\tan(38^\circ))(25/10)\), or use tangent directly in triangle DEF.
content.explanation: Right. Both methods give the exact result \(EF=25\tan(38^\circ)\).

blocks.html:
Independent transfer: make both sketches yourself

Right triangles \(JKL\) and \(MNP\) are similar, with \(J\leftrightarrow M\), \(K\leftrightarrow N\), and \(L\leftrightarrow P\). Angles \(L\) and \(P\) are right angles. Also, \(\angle J=52^\circ\), \(JL=7\), and \(MP=20\).

Find the exact length of \(NP\).

Draw both triangles, place every point label, and mark the corresponding sides. Then choose either the trig-and-scale route or the corresponding-angle shortcut.

Do not calculate a decimal: The correct answer will remain a trig expression.

content.prompt: Which is the exact length of \(NP\)?
content.hint: Corresponding angles are equal in similar triangles — decide which angle of \(MNP\) matches \(52^\circ\). Then name the roles of \(NP\) and \(MP\) from that angle before choosing a ratio.
content.explanation: Correct. \(\tan(52^\circ)=NP/20\), so the exact length is \(NP=20\tan(52^\circ)\). The trig-and-scale route simplifies to the same expression.

content.prompt: Triangle \(DEF\), right angle at \(F\), and the question asks for \(\tan D\). No looking back: what do you draw, what do you label, and what do you check before computing?
choices: Sketch the named vertices; label sides from the right angle; select SOH, CAH, or TOA from the two relevant sides; convert every trig value to a decimal; match Desmos mode to the angle unit; and transfer unchanged ratios across corresponding angles.

Sketch the named vertices; label sides from the chosen acute angle; select SOH, CAH, or TOA from the two relevant sides; preserve the exact trig form; leave Desmos in Radians no matter what the problem states; and scale the ratios by the similar-triangle factor.

Sketch the named vertices; label sides from the chosen acute angle; select SOH, CAH, or TOA from the two relevant sides; preserve the exact trig form; match Desmos mode to the angle unit; and transfer unchanged ratios across corresponding angles.

Label sides from the drawing's orientation; sketch the vertices afterward to confirm; select SOH, CAH, or TOA from the angle sizes; preserve the exact trig form; match Desmos mode to the angle unit; and transfer side lengths unchanged across similar triangles.
content.hint: Recall the sequence: sketch, point labels, side roles, ratio, exact form, mode—and what similarity preserves.
content.explanation: You have it. That process handles SAT point labels, exact trig expressions, unit changes, and combined similar-triangle problems.

content.prompt: In right triangle \(DEF\), the measure of angle \(F\) is \(90^\circ\), \(DF=9\), and \(EF=12\). What is the value of \(\tan D\)?
content.hint: Sketch the named vertices, then label the sides from angle \(D\) — not from the right angle.
content.explanation: Correct. From \(\angle D\), the opposite side is \(EF=12\) and the adjacent side is \(DF=9\), so \(\tan D=\frac{12}{9}=\frac{4}{3}\). \(\frac{3}{4}\) labels the sides from the wrong angle, and the ratios with \(5\) use the hypotenuse \(15\), which tangent never does.

content.html:
Sketch it; label from the angle you're using

The SAT names vertices, not "opposite" and "adjacent" — your sketch does that translating, and then sine, cosine, or tangent is a mechanical pick. Adjacent is never the hypotenuse, and the calculator is in degrees before you press anything.
